Facilities and Capital Expenditures No new or renovated facilities are required to support the launch of this program.
Instruction will be delivered using existing classrooms, instructional laboratories, and online learning infrastructure already available within the College and the University.
These facilities are sufficient to support current enrollment projections and are consistent with the institution’s master plan.
As a result, there are no anticipated capital expenditures associated with facilities for the initial implementation of the program. 2.
Projected Revenues and Tuition/Fee Structure The program will initially leverage existing course capacity, allowing it to be offered with minimal incremental cost.

Students will enroll through existing tuition structures, and no differential tuition is proposed at launch.
This approach is appropriate given that the program primarily utilizes current faculty expertise, courses, and instructional resources.
As enrollment grows and the program matures, the College will evaluate the feasibility of modest program fees or differential tuition to support specialized resources (e.g., cloud-based platforms, proprietary datasets, or experiential learning tools) where appropriate and consistent with University policy.
Any future fees would be designed to be transparent, aligned with student value, and comparable to peer programs, ensuring both affordability and sustainability. 3.

Student Demand.

Demand is expected to come from multiple sources, including current URI students seeking applied, career-relevant skills, working professionals looking to upskill or reskill, and students drawn to interdisciplinary programs that connect business, technology, and societal impact.
Informal indicators such as student interest in related courses and certificates, growing enrollment in adjacent programs, and employer demand for applied analytical and digital skills suggest a steady but manageable level of initial interest.
Projections assume gradual growth as the program gains visibility and establishes a track record.
Regional Competition.
Regionally, there are relatively few programs that combine applied, workforce-oriented content with strong experiential and interdisciplinary elements.
While competing institutions may offer related degrees or certificates, many are either more narrowly technical, less applied, or structured primarily for full-time students.

The program’s design differentiates it through its applied focus, integration with existing strengths at the University, and alignment with regional workforce needs, supporting realistic enrollment assumptions without relying on displacement from peer institutions.
Capacity-Based Assumptions.
Enrollment projections are intentionally aligned with existing instructional and advising capacity in the early years.
Growth assumptions are modest and phased, with increases tied to demonstrated demand and the planned addition of advising support and faculty resources in later stages.
This approach ensures that financial projections are grounded in operational feasibility rather than aspirational targets.
Overall, the enrollment figures used in the financial projections reflect a balanced assessment of student interest, regional competition, and institutional capacity, supporting a financially responsible and sustainable program launch.

Early coursework introduces students to finding and interpreting scholarly and professional sources related to AI and data-driven decision-making.
Upper-level courses emphasize interdisciplinary research, applied problem-solving, and project-based learning, requiring students to integrate library research with hands-on data analysis, modeling, and ethical evaluation.
Writing-intensive courses further support students’ ability to communicate AI-driven insights clearly to technical and non-technical audiences.

Matt Wei, GSO Committee Overview Structure The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (CRCA) consists of six faculty senators and five non-senator research-active faculty.
The Vice President for Research and Economic Development (VPRED) is an ex officio (non-voting) member of the committee.
The Faculty Senate Executive Committee appoints six senators and the VPRED appoints five research-active non-senators to the committee.
The CRCA also comprises a subcommittee, the Competitive Grants Subcommittee.
The CRCA was restructured in 2024 to include non- senators, expanding the committee from 6 to 11 faculty members.
Charge The full committee serves as the representative voice of the university community in all matters related to research, creative, and scholarly activities.
